item.title: The US economy is going backwards. This rally looks bonkers
item.description:
One of the market sayings that always sticks in my mind is that investor sentiment is like holding a beach ball under water – no matter how far down it is, it always wants to pop back up.

We got another reminder of this on Wednesday night, when Wall Street’s S&P 500 rose for the seventh straight session despite new gross domestic product data showing the American economy shrunk in the March quarter, and at a faster rate than expected.

The data is backwards looking and predates US President Donald Trump’s infamous “liberation day” tariff war announcement. But the Donald’s fingerprints were all over this one.

The main driver of the 0.3 per cent contraction in US GDP was what’s called net exports, which is the difference between what America imports and exports. As businesses and consumers rushed to front-run the tariff announcements, imports soared. Imports subtract from the Commerce Department’s calculation of GDP because they represent spending on foreign-made goods and services.

There were other signs of weakness, too, including the slowest growth in consumer spending since 2023 and a fall in government spending thanks to Elon Musk’s cost-cutting efforts. But it’s fitting that this trade war curtain raiser did the damage because the almost inevitable slowdown in America’s June quarter GDP numbers will be all about Trump’s policy agenda.

The effective embargo on Chinese imports is no closer to being removed. So it’s impossible to see how the US avoids a combination of rising prices, shortages of some goods, credit problems among trade-exposed businesses and, ultimately, job losses. That’s not a good environment for consumers and businesses, but it’s poison for corporate profits.

Completely ignoring the recession risk

Not that investors seem to care. Spurred on by a combination of vague noises out of the Trump administration about potential trade deals, reduced volatility, lower bond rates and resilient March quarter earnings, investors have dived back in. The S&P 500’s rally since it bottomed on April 8 is now standing at almost 12 per cent.

In all likelihood, it will keep running into the weekend. Shares in tech giant Microsoft soared in after-hours trade after the company delivered first quarter numbers that beat estimates on revenue and earnings. The stock has climbed more than 5 per cent in the past month in a move broadly representative of big tech’s big bounce back in the past few weeks.

But step back and think about where this rally has taken up. The market is down 5 per cent from the start of the year and 10 per cent since its peak in late February. But we are now back to trading at a price-to-earnings ratio of 20.7 times (and rising), and 2025 earnings growth is still predicted to come in at about 9 per cent.

This is extraordinary and, frankly, a bit bonkers. It completely ignores the recession risk that even the lagging economic data, such as Wednesday night’s GDP figures, is telling us is very real.

As market strategist Marko Kolanovic notes, in a string of recent market crises, including the 2011 European debt crisis, the 2015 emerging markets crisis, the 2018 trade war and the 2022 rate rises that sparked a correction, the P/E ratio fell to 15 times, which is the median valuation since 1985. If the market was to retreat to that valuation now – and Kolanovic says he’s yet to hear a compelling reason why it can’t – then it could fall about 20 per cent from these levels.

Here’s an excellent question

If you doubt this logic, if you believe this time it’s different, believe that trade deals are coming, that the US Federal Reserve will ease (with inflation data out Wednesday night showing core US inflation still at 2.6 per cent, with the tariffs still to really hit), that America’s tech giants can shrug off threats from China, and that earnings can hold up despite a big slowdown and possibly a recession, then Kolanovic has another excellent question for you: how much upside is possible with the S&P 500 sitting at the historically elevated valuation of 20 times earnings?

This rally can’t be ignored. But as strategist Matt King says, investors shouldn’t ignore the fact that the sharemarket bounce has not been complemented with a reversal in the US dollar’s weakness or major selling of the ultimate safe haven asset, gold.

“The optimistic school of thought holds that the Trump put still holds, that tariffs cannot and will not remain in place at elevated levels for extended periods, that terrible sentiment is sending a buy signal, and that fears of de-dollarsation are overblown,” King says.

“But a closer inspection of the data to us suggests the opposite. Tariffs remain an integral and necessary part of Trump’s broader policy agenda, and positions have changed much less than sentiment.”
item.author: James Thomson

item.title: ASX slips; L1 buys Nielson’s stake in Platinum
item.description:
ASX edges lower

The sharemarket snapped its five-day winning streak at the open despite a dramatic reversal on Wall Street that saw the S&P 500 finish higher on the day, as miners dragged.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index edged down 0.2 per cent, or by 13.8 points, in the first few minutes of trading. The All Ordinaries edged down 0.1 per cent. Just three sectors were in the red with miners leading losses.

More to follow

L1 Capital buys Platinum stake from Neilson

Platinum founder Kerr Neilson has sold a half of a 19.9 per cent stake in the ASX-listed fund manager to L1 Capital, according to substantial disclosures filed with the market operator.

The Melbourne hedge fund manager paid 54¢ each for 56 million Platinum shares owned by Neilson, worth $30.2 million. L1 has also been granted a call option to acquire another 59.85 million shares.

The platinum shares closed at 57¢ on Wednesday, valuing the company at $330 million. Neilson founded Platinum in 1994.

Woodside gives Worley two-year contract extension

Worley has been given a two-year extension to its contract, with Woodside to provide brownfield engineering and procurement services covering two gas plants.

Under the agreement, Worley will continue to provide project management, front-end engineering, detailed design and procurement services for onshore brownfield projects required by Woodside.

The work will focus on Woodside’s Karratha gas plant and King Bay supply base, as well as the Pluto liquified natural gas plant. Worley has been servicing the projects since 2018.

GPT AUM rises $800m

GPT added $800 million in assets under management in the March quarter, bringing total assets to $34.7 billion after its joint venture with the Perron Group boosted its retail AUM.

The shopping centre owner said it was on track to hit full-year guidance of funds from operations per security growth of 1 to 3 per cent and a distribution per security of 24¢.

Robinhood tops estimates amid volatility as crypto slows

Retail investors flocked to Robinhood Markets as US President Donald Trump’s global tariffs roiled markets, boosting the company’s revenue and earnings, even as growth in cryptocurrency revenue slowed.

Total net revenue jumped 50 per cent from a year earlier to $US927 million ($1.4 billion), while net income more than doubled to $US336 million. Per-share earnings of 37 cents topped analysts’ estimates of 33 cents.

“We started the year off strong, driving market share gains,” chief financial officer Jason Warnick said in a statement Wednesday. “It’s also great to see strong customer engagement to start Q2.”

The company increased its share repurchase authorisation by $US500 million to $US1.5 billion, “reflecting management and the board’s confidence in our financial strength and future growth prospects,” Warnick said.

Through April 25, 20 million shares have been bought back for a total of $US667 million, the company said.

Sims shelves waste tech project, sees $25m hit

Sims expects a $25 million hit from its decision to stop developing plasma-assisted gasification technology for the processing of automotive shredder residue waste.

The metals recycling company said it had conducted a market assessment of the technical and market viability of the technology and concluded market conditions were “not yet conducive to scaling [it]”.

Sims said archiving the product would align with its capital discipline and cost reduction program. Closure-related costs are expected to be $4 million in the second half of the financial year. Sims also expects to report a non-cash write-off charge of around $21 million.

Woolworths e-commerce sales surge

Woolworths’ e-commerce sales surged 15.7 per cent to $2.2 billion in the first quarter, driving a marginal rise in group sales.

Group sales, which rose 3.2 per cent year-on-year to $17.3 billion, were tempered by lower sales from Big W. That prompted the supermarket group to revise down its half-year profit outlook for Big W to a loss of $70 million. Australian food sales rose 3.6 per cent year-on-year.

“While the market remains competitive and consumer outlook uncertain, we are making progress [on our priorities set out in February] and will provide a more detailed update at our full-year results in August” chief executive Amanda Bardwell said.

Resolute adds West Africa gold assets with $235m deal

Resolute Mining has agreed to buy two West African undeveloped gold projects from AngloGold Ashanti for US$150 million ($235 million), marking the latest in a flurry of deals in the sector.

The ASX-listed miner will pay for the Doropo and ABC mines in Côte d’Ivoire in three instalments, comprising US$25 million in cash upfront and US$125 million in two other instalments. The deal also involves Resolute transferring its exploration permits in Guinea to AngloGold, as well as other royalty payments.

The Doropo project is located in the northeast of Côte d’Ivoire, and when operational is expected to produce an average of 167,000 ounces annually at an average cost of $US1,047 each.

Gold recently breached $US3500 per ounce, with some observers tipping it to hit $US4000 in the coming months.

“The development of the Doropo Project is expected to materially increase Resolute’s annual gold production to above 500,000 ounces, complementing the company’s existing operations, the Syama mine in Mali and the Mako mine in Senegal,” the miner said.

Resolute was victim to a shakedown in neighbouring Mali last year when the military junta detained its former chief executive and other staff, forcing the miner to pay a US$160 million ransom.

Spark NZ addresses Street Talk report

Spark New Zealand said on Thursday no transaction had been agreed with a co-investor for its data centre portfolio after it had launched an auction seeking an investment partner for the portfolio, which could be worth as much as $NZ1.2 billion ($1.1 billion).

New Zealand’s largest telecommunications company said in a statement: “no transaction has been agreed and a transaction (including any value) is not yet certain.

“As was communicated in a H1 trading update, Spark has commenced a process to explore interest from prospective partners to support further data centre investment”.

Top stories

| The Coalition is promising to reduce the budget deficit by more than $10 billion over the next four years, and to lower debt by $40 billion.

| A stake in Thinking Machines Lab – valued at more than $15 billion – is in high demand. At least two local firms have secured one.

| In the heavily Asian populated seat of Bennelong, Scott Yung has told voters who may not like Peter Dutton that he won’t be the opposition leader forever.

| Labor and Liberal strategists believe a huge number of key seats remain on a knife edge just days out from polling day.

| After Media Watch blasted his involvement helping performer Austen Tayshus secure ABC interviews, Kim Williams reflects on a year in the ABC chair.

US futures positive after Meta, Microsoft report

US futures were positive at the start of trade after Meta and Microsoft reported quarterly revenues that came ahead of expectations and cleared fears of any immediate impact of US tariffs on demand and sales.

Contracts for the technology-heavy Nasdaq Index were up 16.5 points while the S&P 500 Index was up 3.3 points. Traders took the technology giants’ earnings as good news for US businesses, fearing US President Donald Trump’s punitive tariff regime could hurt demand and spark price increases due to the tariff-induced strain on supply chains.

The Nasdaq closed marginally lower, down 0.1 per cent, in regular trading hours. The main S&P 500 index pared an earlier loss to close 0.2 per cent higher.
item.author: Natasha Rudra, Nicola Blackburn

item.title: ASX rebound is more hedge fund trading than recovery, strategists warn
item.description:
The rapid rebound in the sharemarket last month from the Trump administration’s disruptive tariff plans was driven by hedge funds exiting their bearish stock bets strategists say, warning that the recovery was likely unsustainable.

After a volatile month triggered by erratic policy announcements from the US president Donald Trump, major stock indices from the ASX to Wall Street have largely returned to levels before the “Liberation Day” tariff shock on April 2 erased trillions of dollars in market value.

Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 Index has climbed to a two-month high this week, having rebounded around 3.2 per cent from the sharp sell-off at the start of the month. On Wall Street, the Nasdaq Composite is up 1.3 per cent and the S&P 500 is down just 0.9 per cent since April 2.

Wilsons Advisory’s head of investment strategy, David Cassidy, said investor positioning had got quite extreme after Trump’s reciprocal tariffs raised fears of a recession. He said the recent rally was more a function of hedge funds rapidly unwinding short bets.

“I think [it’s been] fast money, a sort of reflexive positioning-driven rally rather than anything truly fundamental,” Cassidy told The Australian Financial Review.

“People were very quick to short very quickly, and now that’s been reversed. I’d still have concerns that there’s a fair bit of economic fallout to come through over the next few weeks.”

Cassidy said while he wasn’t “uber” bearish on the outlook for global growth and the market, he was cautious over the next three months given the risk of a “pretty scary run” of US economic data.

“It’s hard to have a longer-term view,” he said, before noting Trump’s significant walk-back from his initial Draconian policies. “I think possibly there is a path out of this, but it’s just hard at the moment to think that it’s all over, and it’s off to the races just yet.”

Bell Potter strategist Richard Coppleson also noted this week in his daily report to clients that there had been a significant unwind in short positions in the market. A short position is when people make money on a security’s decline.

No blue skies

“I have not seen the shorts rally this much for a long time, it has usually occurred right before a big run in them, as those shorts suddenly see that things have changed,” he said.

“New factors are now impacting their thesis.”

Perpetual’s head of investment strategy, Matt Sherwood, said investors should remain vigilant about the outlook for economic growth.

“We have to keep in mind that valuations are still expensive and there is a major growth slowdown coming, so investors need to brace for impact and not be sucked into this rally we are seeing in recent weeks,” he said.

“There’s still a big growth hole. I doubt whether America could announce any major trade deals within the 90-day moratorium. I still think that the markets are far too optimistic about the path ahead.”

Sherwood said the challenge for ASX investors was not so much the outlook for global growth, but more valuations given the sharemarket was still “trading expensively” despite heightened uncertainty.

“That’s a very brave investor [who is] is blindly following the Australian sharemarket trends thinking it’s only blue skies ahead.”

Joseph Koh, a portfolio manager at Blackwattle Investment Partners, said investors had become “complacent” given the uncertainty from the trade war.

He said the outlook of the sharemarket was more skewed towards the “downside”, especially as corporate earnings, particularly those with international exposure, were likely to “take a hit” from the tariffs.

Since the trade war kicked off, he has added to existing domestic-focused companies such as Charter Hall and Seven Group.

UBS has also tempered its sharemarket outlook and this week slashed its year-end target for the ASX 200 to 8150 from 8850 previously, implying the benchmark index will barely move from current levels.

Strategist Richard Schellbach said the ASX had run ahead of “softening underlying fundamentals” and warned of a looming wave of earnings downgrades from the deteriorating global economic backdrop.

“We expect the upcoming period of trading updates and quarterlies from Aussie companies to be unfavourable in both tone and guidance revisions, and thus expect to see earnings downgrades from consensus analysts,” Schellbach wrote in a note to clients.
item.author: Joanne Tran, Sarah Jones

item.title: Bond market too optimistic about rapid rate cuts, investors warn
item.description:
Inflation has finally returned to the Reserve Bank of Australia’s target band for the first time since the COVID-19 pandemic, but fund managers warn that lingering price pressures should curb hopes for deeper easing.

Bond traders fully expect the central bank to cut the cash rate by a quarter-point rate to 3.85 per cent when it meets on May 20 after data showed core inflation – the RBA’s preferred measure – cooled to 2.9 per cent in the March quarter from 3.3 per cent, within the 2 per cent to 3 per cent target. Inflation peaked at nearly 7 per cent in 2022.

“This is a significant further improvement from prior periods and should keep the RBA on track to continue cutting rates in May,” said Charlie Jamieson, chief investment officer at Jamieson Coote Bonds. The bond fund manager expects at least three cuts by Christmas.

The shining light in the economic data was a decline in services inflation. “Seeing that will be a big relief for the RBA,” added Fortlake Asset Management co-founder Christian Baylis.

Yet because the consumer price index came in above consensus forecast of 2.8 per cent, markets have trimmed bets of an outsized half-a-point reduction by the RBA to a less than one-in-10 chance.

Earlier this month, bond traders were pricing in an almost 50:50 chance the RBA would deliver a jumbo rate cut after US President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariff threats raised concern about the global growth outlook.

Caution

Money markets are still nearly fully priced for five 25 basis points cuts this year, but investors and strategists doubt it will be that many.

“The RBA will remain cautious and data-dependent, which suggests a follow-up cut in July is not guaranteed,” said IFM chief economist Alex Joiner.

He said August seemed a more likely option as further clarity on the global economic environment emerges.

RBA Governor Michele Bullock has called for patience as policymakers assess how the new US tariff regime could alter global supply and demand. The central bank cut the cash rate in February for the first time in nearly five years but paused this month, just one day before Trump’s April 2 hefty tariff announcement.

Andrew Lilley, chief rate strategist at Barrenjoey, said there was no pressure for the RBA to deliver back-to-back rate cuts because inflation was unlikely to undershoot.

“The most likely thing the RBA would do is cut in May, cut in August, and then sit and wait,” he said.

Some pundits still question whether a rate cut in May is a sure thing.

‘No desperate need’

Perpetual’s head of investment strategy, Matt Sherwood, said the “not small” inflation pulse from Saturday’s federal election and the uncertainty of the trade war could hold back the RBA.

Labor and the Coalition have pledged cost-of-living relief measures, which will add to inflationary pressures.

Baylis ascribes a 60 per cent chance of a May rate cut because the job market was still strong. He said while inflation was moving in the right direction, there was no “desperate need” to cut instantaneously.

“I wouldn’t say May is an absolute done deal, but if I had to call something, I’d call a cut,” he added.

Muddying the outlook is the prospect of a bigger global trade war, which could impact inflation and trigger a global recession.

“The RBA may want to see the results of those opposing forces,” added Baylis.

The Australian dollar climbed 0.5 per cent to US64.10¢, nearing a five-month peak of US64.49¢ touched on Tuesday. In the physical bond markets, the three-year rate, which reflects interest rate expectations, initially ticked up 3 basis points before returning to 3.31 per cent. The 10-year return lost 2 basis points to 4.12 per cent.
item.author: Cecile Lefort

item.title: Inflation steady; $100b fund’s Trump plan; Ex-model running for One Nation
item.description:
Want to get this in your inbox at lunchtime every weekday? Financial Review subscribers can sign up for The Brief newsletter here. Plus start your day with our Before the Bell newsletter and read a full wrap of the day’s news in Market Wrap.

In today’s news, inflation is holding steady, new Cbus chief investment officer Leigh Gavin has a plan for Donald Trump’s trade wars, and a former Italian model is running for One Nation.

Making news

Annual inflation steady in Q1 at 2.4pc, above forecast
Shares were up 0.3 per cent near noon AEST, extending a two-month high buoyed by tech stocks. Annual CPI ticked up 2.9 per cent in the first quarter, from 3.3 per cent. Follow live updates.

‘Dog’s breakfast’: Dutton hits out at Ryan’s campaign
Peter Dutton says Monique Ryan has selective memory loss; Treasurer Jim Chalmers addresses the media. Follow live updates.

Meet the former Italian model running for One Nation
Bianca Colecchia, 32, says the first question she usually gets at pre-poll booths is: “How can you run for One Nation when you are a migrant yourself?”

The two worrying trends revealed in Australia’s AAA warning
The next federal government should be thinking about ways to get control of the financially imprudent behaviour of the state and territory governments.

Meet the ex-Deloitte consultant who has driven 85,000km to win a seat
Tom Venning has a strong chance to be the new MP for a sprawling South Australian electorate after exiting the corporate world to bring a back-to-basics economic approach.

If Dutton’s path to victory cuts through Sydney, he has problems
In conversations with voters from Gordon to Liverpool, cost of living and housing featured again and again – but few blamed Labor and Albanese for the price rises.

Around the world

Trump celebrates 100 days in office by bashing Powell, touting tariffs
Donald Trump criticised Federal Reserve chairman Jerome Powell despite assurances this month that he did not plan to fire him over interest rate cuts.

Trump calls Bezos after reports Amazon would show tariff charges on its site
The retailer spent a chaotic morning denying a report that it planned to display prices detailing the levies’ impact on Amazon.com.

GM delays investor call, UPS axes 20,000 jobs as tariffs create chaos
About 40 companies worldwide have pulled or lowered their forward guidance in the first two weeks of the first-quarter earnings season.

Mark Carney’s Liberals only narrowly miss out on a majority
With final results coming in from nearly all districts, the Liberals secured 169 seats in the 343-member parliament, just three shy of gaining outright rule.

Matter of opinion

He’s just taken over a $100b fund. Here’s his trade war plan
New Cbus chief investment officer Leigh Gavin says Donald Trump’s attack on 20 years of globalisation will make life harder for super members, writes Chanticleer.

Banks can’t afford to bust the defensive myth propping up share prices
It’s amazing how we all get sucked into short-term market narratives. Do we really think highly leveraged financial institutions are safe havens? Surely, it’s a fad, writes Chanticleer.

Business life

High-powered Sydney couple finds new success importing wines
A lawyer and a project manager paused their careers to champion Europe’s best female drink producers.

The fashion CEO who doesn’t look at her phone until she gets to the office
Australian Fashion Council chief Jaana Quaintance-James makes a point of staying away from her mobile when walking to and from work, and reading.

What your height says about your health
Younger generations have been getting taller as living standards have shifted, childhood starvation disappeared, and common infectious diseases were eradicated.

item.title: He’s just taken over a $100b fund. Here’s his trade war plan
item.description:
The first 100 days of Donald Trump’s second White House stint has just delivered the biggest loss on Wall Street for the start of a presidential term since Richard Nixon in 1973. So perhaps it’s no surprise that new Cbus chief investment officer Leigh Gavin takes just seconds to reel off the number of days Trump has left.

Gavin doesn’t expect the rollercoaster to end anytime soon.

“We would imagine the next 1361 days are going to have similar patterns, as we move from markets perhaps getting overconfident that the genie can be put back in the bottle, to getting overly concerned that things have changed and changed forever,” he tells Chanticleer.

“But there’s certainly a secular change to how the US views itself and how the US views itself in the context of global trade. The thematics of deglobalisation and the move to mercantilism are not going away.”

That’s not good news for investor returns, which won’t enjoy the same tailwinds of cheap money, rising asset prices and generally low inflation they’ve known for the past 20 years. So the challenge for Australian superannuation funds is to work out how they see the world, and particularly the US, after a brutal few months on markets.

Gavin says Cbus was mildly underweight US stocks through last year “and that underweight had got bigger as 2024 went along”. Happily, the fund was long Europe at the same time.

“That’s played out pretty well during the first four months of the year,” he says. “We weren’t sure what was going to push the EU and countries like Germany into more stimulatory fiscal policy. Turns out it was Donald Trump. You might not have predicted that four months ago.”

But Gavin says investors write off America at their peril. It remains the centre of global innovation and entrepreneurialism, and that needs to be weighed up against the changes Trump has brought about.

“It’s been the best country at turning GDP growth into earnings per share growth over the last 15 years in particular, and I don’t think that’s going to dramatically change over the next 15 years,” he says. “But the world is clearly moving to a different place, and exactly where it lands, we’ll probably find out quite a lot over the next few months. I would say at the end of this four-year term that the US is going to be in a different position from where it started.”

How does a $100 billion fund allocate assets given that level of uncertainty? Gavin says the fund’s equity allocation is about 3 per cent lower than it was at the end of December, and the fund is generally more cautious about the broader environment. But as markets reached what Gavin describes as over-sold levels recently, Cbus tried to add equity exposure.

The window closed quickly. While it has bought stocks at the margin, an impressive six-day rise in the S&P 500 has now pushed the market up more than 11 per cent.

More broadly, Gavin is guided by three big ideas. First, the fund’s diversification, particularly its exposure to unlisted private assets, has been a key driver of returns over decades and can be again as the bumper performance from US equities in the past two years fades.

Second, Gavin wants to have the capacity to take advantage of opportunities that might emerge from dislocation, and so the fund’s cash levels are running a bit higher than usual. The lessons of the COVID-19 pandemic are firmly in Gavin’s mind – Cbus bought two shopping centres during the period at very attractive prices and has done well on both.

Finally, while Gavin is prepared to be tactical when appropriate, he says the fund’s 900,000 members expect it to remain focused on the long term. “You can chase your tail a lot in this environment by trying to work out what the next Trump tweet is going to do for markets. Making wholesale changes to the portfolio based on Twitter is not a great way for a long-term investor like ourselves to run.”

Gavin replaces Brett Chatfield, who was appointed less than two years ago and will depart to become the chief investment officer of an unnamed family office. It adds to the high level of executive turnover at the fund, against the backdrop of scandals at one of its sponsor unions, the CFMEU, and scrutiny from both the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority and Australian Securities and Investments Commission.

Alexandra Campbell resigned as deputy investment officer last May, around the same time the head of total portfolio management Mark Ferguson also left. Chief strategy officer Alexandra West left a few months later, prompting a critical assessment from research and ratings house Morningstar.

Gavin, who joined Cbus in mid-2023 after stints at AustralianSuper, LUCRF Super as chief investment officer, and Frontier Advisers, insists the investment team has been insulated from the regulatory scrutiny and is in good shape after a series of recent hires. These include Matt Kempton as head of equity strategies, Justin Pascoe as head of portfolio construction, Jordan Kraiten as head of private markets and infrastructure, and former Cooper Investors fund manager Ryan Riedler to run the ASX core strategy.

Cbus is three years into a five-year plan to increase the internalisation of its investment management from about 35 per cent at present to 50 per cent, but Gavin says he has no plans at this stage to follow funds such as AustralianSuper in setting up overseas offices, arguing global investments can still be run effectively from Australia.

The Cbus investment team is in the middle of its annual planning cycle, which involves no shortage of stress testing and scenario planning. Clearly, Gavin says, the investment committee wants to be sure about the assumptions used to judge deals today.

The base case is that things get tougher from here for investors and super fund members. Twenty years of globalisation have been great for investor returns, and the series of bilateral trade deals the Trump administration seems to envisage will create an environment that’s simply more complex for investors.

There will still be opportunities for active management to find pockets of above-market returns, but super fund members won’t enjoy the same secular tailwinds beneath their wings.

“If the Trump administration continues on with what they’ve announced in the first 100 days, we’re certainly moving to a more challenging investment environment for beta, but I still think there are opportunities for alpha,” says Gavin.

item.title: ASX hits first monthly gain since January; CBA nears record
item.description:
ASX extends rally; CBA nears record

The Australian sharemarket recorded its first monthly gain since January, taking its cues from Wall Street overnight as investors shrugged off weak US data, betting that equities would weather a slowdown in economic growth cause by the US tariffs.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 0.7 per cent, or by 55.6 points, to 8126.2 points for its fifth day of gains and extended its monthly gain to 3.6 per cent. The All Ordinaries rose 0.6 per cent on the day as seven of the 11 sectors finished in the green, with technology leading the advance.

Sentiment was buoyed by US trading after the S&P 500 Index climbed for the sixth session despite a fall in US job openings in March and a plunge in consumer. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signalled progress on trade deals with countries such as Japan and India, which also helped.

Pendulum swings

But US futures are pointing lower ahead of earnings from US megacaps Microsoft and Meta. Key US inflation and GDP data is also expected after the market close to help gauge how the US economy fared in March before US President Donald Trump’s sweeping “liberation day” tariffs.

“The market is like a pendulum swinging at the moment – and it hasn’t quite found equilibrium,” VanEck head of investments Russel Chesler cautioned. “Trump gave it a push, it was swaying rapidly from side to side – and now the range is narrower, but we still don’t know where it’s all going to settle”.

Still, gains for rate-sensitive technology companies and the banks helped the ASX extend its rebound from recent lows. Index giant Commonwealth Bank rose 2.2 per cent to $166.60, inching back towards its record high of $168, and TechnologyOne and WiseTech advanced 2.5 per cent to $30.06 and 1.1 per cent to $88.52, respectively.

Those gains tussled with losses from miners as gold stocks tracked a further fall in prices. The spot price neared $US3310 an ounce. Newmont retreated 1.7 per cent to $82.07 and Evolution 2 per cent to $7.83.

Stocks in focus

Investors continued to dump Northern Star Resources after the gold miner lowered its full-year output guidance, citing higher maintenance costs and royalties. The shares closed down 3.5 per cent at $19.18.

The more defensive areas of the market were sold off, including utilities. Origin retreated 1.4 per cent to $10.64 after reporting a quarter-on-quarter fall in LNG revenue.

Coles edged down 0.8 per cent to $21.22 despite sales from its Coles Finest range jumping 13.7 per cent in the three months to March 30.

Ora Banda Mining lost 6.1 per cent to 99.5¢ after lowering its full-year production guidance.

Alcoa retreated 1.7 per cent to $38.95 after Spain’s nationwide power outage on Monday affected operations at its San Ciprian smelter.

Mark Mobius says fund holds 95pc in cash because of trade war chaos

Veteran emerging markets investor Mark Mobius has kept the bulk of his funds’ holdings in cash, given that the trade-related uncertainty is likely to persist for up to six months.

“At this stage, cash is king. So 95 per cent of my money in the funds are in cash,” Mobius said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Wednesday. “Right now, we got to keep the cash and be ready to move when the time is right.”

Mobius, who has been investing in developing markets for about three decades, said some emerging market countries such as India would do quite well in this environment, “but we have to wait until all of this evens out and we see a settling down of this uncertainty”.

Investors would probably be able to assess market opportunities only once the trade negotiations took place over the next four to six months, he said.

Mobius said he would not hold so much cash for “more than three to four months” and would start to deploy some of the funds depending on where the opportunities were.

“If the market comes down further, of course we will put more money in,” said the co-founder of Mobius Capital Partners.

UBS tips more bad news for Macquarie

UBS is forecasting a weaker full-year earnings result from Macquarie that it expects will amount to further earnings downgrades for the investment bank.

Noting it was “a difficult business to forecast”, UBS is forecasting a full-year net profit of $3.4 billion, lower than consensus estimates for a $3.7 billion. It pointed to the ongoing lack of asset realisations from the investment bank’s Green Investment Group and weaker revenues from commodities and global markets.

“The market continues to look through a number of soft prints and earnings misses for Macquarie over the past 12 months and we expect further earnings downgrades on the back of FY25,” UBS added.

UBS pointed to one ‘positive development’ – Macquarie’s intended sale of its North American and European public investments business to Nomura.

Macquarie shares were down 1.1 per cent around 3.20pm on Wednesday. UBS has a neutral rating on the stock and a price target of $235 a share.

Morgan Stanley singles out AMP, tips wealth recovery

Morgan Stanley has singled out AMP as its preferred pick among the wealth managers at a time when improving flows, more longevity solutions and lighter regulation should all support the sector’s recovery, the broker says.

Morgan Stanley forecast more than a 30 per cent upside for AMP, but revised its price target lower to $1.62 from $1.76.

For AMP, improving flows into the wealth management arm, and Morgan Stanley’s view that there is further potential for cost-outs in superannuation and investment, would support the stock’s re-rating, the broker said.

AMP is Morgan Stanley’s preferred pick over peers Challenger and Insignia Financial.

ASX to reset two-month high; Newmont down 2pc

The Australian sharemarket held gains on Wednesday, taking its cues from Wall Street as investors shrugged off weak US data, betting that equities can weather a slowdown in economic growth from tariffs.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index lifted 0.3 per cent, or by 23.2 points, to 8093.8 points near 2pm, extending its highest level in two months. The All Ordinaries rose 0.3 per cent. Six of 11 sectors were in the green with real estate leading the advance.

The S&P 500 Index climbed for a sixth session despite a fall in US job openings in March and a plunge in consumer. Sentiment was buoyed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signalling progress on trade deals with countries including Japan and India. But US futures are pointing lower after disappointing earnings from Super Micro Computer.

AMP head of investment strategy Shane Oliver cautioned markets could still retest their year-to-date lows despite the rally in recent days. “If we see weaker economic data ahead, I’d be wary about stocks going off to the races again,” he said.

Gains for rate-sensitive real estate companies and the banks buoyed the ASX. Index bellwether Commonwealth Bank rose 1.5 per cent. Goodman Group rose 1.4 per cent and data centre play DigiCo added 2.4 per cent.

Those gains tussled with losses from miners tracking falling iron ore and gold prices. Gold heavyweight Newmont retreated 1.9 per cent and Evolution was off 2.2 per cent. Among the iron ore producers, Fortescue dropped 1.7 per cent.

The more defensive areas of the market were sold off, including utilities. Origin retreated 1.8 per cent after reporting a quarter-on-quarter fall in LNG revenue.

Stocks on the move

In other corporate news, Ora Banda Mining sank 7.1 per cent after lowering its full-year production guidance, owing to downtime at its processing plant from equipment upgrades.

Star Entertainment shares were flat even as its losses ballooned in the third quarter to $21 million, up from $8 million in the second quarter.

Champion Iron edged down 0.9 per cent despite reporting a record quarter for sales in the three months to March, rising 18 per cent from a year earlier to 3.5 million dry metric tonnes.

And Alcoa retreated 1.6 per cent after Spain’s nationwide power outage on Monday affected operations at its San Ciprian smelter.

Canada eyes bumper year for Australian mining IPOs

Canada’s largest stock exchange expects a bumper year of dual listings of Australian companies after a record 12 months, as domestic resources explorers and energy developers search for bigger pools of investor money.

Robert Peterman, the director of global business development at the Toronto Stock Exchange, said that Australia had been “the No.1 market for us”, particularly for mining companies looking for funding.

Over the past 10 months, seven Australian companies – including Perth gold explorer Westgold Resources, copper hopeful Firefly Metals, and uranium producer Paladin Energy – have listed on the Toronto bourse.

Northern Star sell-off continues

Investors continued dumping shares in Northern Star Resources on Wednesday after the gold mining giant lowered its output guidance for the 2025 financial year, citing higher maintenance costs and higher royalties.

Northern Star shares were down 3.6 per cent near 1pm, notching the fourth-biggest loss on the S&P/ASX 200 Index. The stock had closed 4.7 per cent lower on Tuesday to $19.88 after the announcement.

The gold miner reported softer-than-expected production in the third quarter, at 388,000 ounces. Analysts at Macquarie downgraded its 2026 output forecast for the gold miner to 1.9 million ounces that year. Northern Star maintained its forecast for 2 million ounces.

Chinese AI stocks advance

Shares of Chinese smart-device manufacturers rose after President Xi Jinping visited an artificial intelligence innovation centre in Shanghai.

YingTong Telecommunication, which makes wireless acoustic parts and bluetooth headphones used in AI glasses, jumped by the 10 per cent limit in Shenzhen. Minami Acoustics and Shenzhen Rapoo Technology, which manufacture consumer electronics parts, each gained more than 6 per cent.

China’s prime-time news program on Wednesday led with a four-minute segment on Xi’s visit to an incubator and accelerator for AI tech firms, and showed footage of him trying on a pair of AI glasses. It also included a shot of a pair of StarV View spectacles, developed by Chinese maker DreamSmart. Xi praised Shanghai’s AI development, according to the report.

AI stocks in Shanghai have weakened in the past couple of months after a strong rally fuelled by optimism around DeepSeek products – with performance stunted by expensive valuations coupled with concerns about US tariffs. The CSI Artificial Intelligence Index is 17 per cent off this year’s highs from February.

China factory activity shrinks the most since 2023

China’s factory activity slipped into the worst contraction since December 2023, revealing early damage to the world’s second-biggest economy from the trade war with the US.

The official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index was 49 compared with 50.5 in March, the National Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday. That was lower than the median forecast of 49.7 by economists. Any number below 50 points to a contraction.

The non-manufacturing measure of activity in construction and services fell to 50.4 from 50.8 last month. That compares with a forecast of 50.6. The onshore stock benchmark CSI 300 Index was little changed.

The latest PMI readings offer the first official look at the health of China’s economy after the Trump administration imposed sweeping tariffs of 145 per cent on Chinese products, a level expected to hurt a sector that contributed nearly a third of the economy’s growth last year.

RBA yet to ‘sharpen knife’ on rate cuts: VanEck

Core inflation needs to stay within the Reserve Bank’s target range for a sustained period before markets can be sure it will “sharpen the knife” on rate cuts, according to VanEck head of investments and capital markets Russel Chesler.

While calling a rate cut next month “the most likely outcome”, Chesler said the current picture of Australia’s economy meant a reduction was not yet “strictly necessary”.

“We would like to see a longer run of the trimmed mean being within the RBA’s target 2 to 3 per cent range before we start sharpening the knife for further rate cuts,” he said, adding Australia’s inflation was nevertheless “encouraging”.

Banks, tech buoy ASX; Origin drops

The Australian sharemarket edged higher at lunchtime, taking its cues from Wall Street as investors shrugged off weak US data betting that the equities can weather a slowdown in economic growth from tariffs.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 0.2 per cent, or by 17.1 points, to 8087.70 points near 12pm, extending its highest level in two months. The All Ordinaries rose 0.2 per cent. Six of 11 sectors were in the green with technology leading the advance.

The S&P 500 Index climbed for a sixth session despite a fall in US job openings in March and a plunge in consumer.

Sentiment was buoyed by US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent signalling progress on trade deals with countries including Japan and India. But US futures are pointing lower after disappointing earnings from Super Micro Computer.

AMP head of investment strategy Shane Oliver cautioned markets could still retest their year-to-date lows, despite the rally in recent days. “If we see weaker economic data ahead, I’d be wary about stocks going off to the races again,” he said.

On the ASX, gains from rate sensitive technology companies and the banks helped buoyed the market. Index bellwether Commonwealth Bank rose 1.3 per cent while Westpac added 0.8 per cent. WiseTech advanced 1 per cent and TechnologyOne 1.2 per cent.

The more defensive areas of the market were sold off including utilities. Origin retreated 1.6 per cent after reporting a quarter-on-quarter fall in LNG revenue.

Stocks on the move

In other corporate news, Ora Banda Mining sank 6.4 per cent after lowering its full-year production guidance, owing to downtime at its processing plant from equipment upgrades.

Star Entertainment added 1.9 per cent even as its losses ballooned in the third quarter to $21 million, up from $8 million in the second quarter.

Champion Iron dropped 2 per cent despite reporting a record quarter for sales in the three months to March, rising 18 per cent to 3.5 million dry metric tonnes from a year earlier.

And Alcoa retreated 1.1 per cent after Spain’s nationwide power outage on Monday affected operations at its San Ciprián smelter.

item.title: Canada eyes bumper year for Aussie mining IPOs
item.description:
Canada’s largest stock exchange expects a bumper year of dual listings of Australian companies after a record 12 months, as local resources explorers and energy developers search for bigger pools of investor money.

Robert Peterman, the director of global business development at the Toronto Stock Exchange, said Australia had been “the number-one market for us”, particularly for mining companies looking for funding.

Over the past 10 months, seven Australian companies – including Perth gold explorer Westgold Resources, copper hopeful Firefly Metals and uranium producer Paladin Energy – have listed on the Toronto bourse.

This year, gold producer Alkane Resources is pursuing a secondary listing in Toronto after announcing its $559 million acquisition of Canada’s Mandalay Resources. Lithium explorer Mont Royal Resources revealed similar plans following a merger with North America’s Commerce Resources, adding to the 26 companies now listed in both Toronto and Sydney.

“The [Toronto Stock Exchange] was the biggest market in the world last year for new mining listings for raising capital, so companies come to Toronto to access that capital,” Peterman said in an interview during a visit to Sydney.

More than $C10 billion ($11.2 billion) was raised by the mining sector on the Toronto exchange last year, accounting for nearly half of the exchange’s total capital raised, compared with the ASX’s $C7.2 billion. While both the Toronto Stock Exchange and the ASX host hundreds of natural resources companies, Toronto is bigger than Australia. “If you want access to the number-one market for mining capital in 2024, you need a listing on TSX,” said Peterman.

For Hugh Dive, investment chief at Atlas Funds Management, the growing trend of gold companies listing in Canada is unsurprising, given the country’s investors’ deep expertise in precious metals.

“As a country, they have a high-risk tolerance for gold and uranium as they understand them better than a lot of Australians,” he said. In contrast, Australia was more familiar with commodities such as iron ore and coal, said Dive, who started his investment career in Vancouver.

Arbitrage play

Dual listings, Dive said, offer issuers valuable flexibility, particularly on days when a stock price takes a hit in Sydney. “Australian investors may be more circumspect on the company, whereas Canadians may not,” he said.

Despite the White House’s erratic trade agenda, Peterman remains bullish on the long-term prospects for the mining sector, particularly junior miners – small, early-stage mining companies that focus on exploration.

Unlike Australia, Toronto hosts a separate exchange – TSX Venture – catering to early-stage companies, including those still in the exploration phase. Peterman said junior miners could improve their valuations by accelerating permitting processes and refining project execution, especially as demand for critical metals, such as copper, continues to rise. These companies, taking on significant financial risks to discover new deposits, often become acquisition targets once promising finds are made.

“Most people believe that energy transition will be one of the most important themes in the capital markets over the next five years,” he said.

Capital access is a key reason why companies flock to Toronto, particularly in sectors such as gold, silver and copper, where Canadian markets have a strong track record. This was a driving factor for Southern Cross Gold to list on the Toronto Stock Exchange earlier this year.

“It has a much better capital base that backs exploration stories,” said Southern Cross chief executive Michael Hudson, describing the North American market as larger, more dynamic, and more willing to take risks than investors in Australia. “Exploration is better rewarded, as opposed to mining stories that are probably better understood in Australia.”

Among his shareholders is Pierre Lassonde, the Quebecois former president of Newmont Mining, who transformed the gold royalty business model.

However, listing in Canada is not without its challenges. One notable drawback is the lack of transparency compared to Australia. Hudson said he often found it difficult to track who was buying or selling shares in his company due to the Toronto exchange’s anonymous category on its share registry. “In Australia, you can manage your capital structure much more effectively. It is a much more transparent and open market,” he said.

The investor landscape in Canada also contrasts sharply with Australia, particularly when it comes to large pension funds, which tend to steer clear of the mining sector. Despite both countries having substantial retirement funds, Hudson pointed out that Australian self-managed superannuation funds are far more active participants in the market, while industry funds typically focus on the larger, more established companies.

As Hudson noted, many Canadians look across at Australia and observe, “Look, they’re investing in their own future.”

Canada’s main benchmark is up 0.3 per cent so far this year, having outperformed its Australian rival, which slipped 2 per cent, as well as the United States’ S&P 5000, down nearly 6 per cent.
item.author: Cecile Lefort

item.title: Global investors pile into ASX giants amid Wall Street exodus
item.description:
Uncertainty about the outlook for the world’s largest economy is pushing major investors to shift funds out of the United States and into some of Australia’s largest companies, buoying the local sharemarket.

The mass re-allocation of capital has been triggered by the Trump administration’s aggressive trade policies, which have prompted investors to question America’s economic dominance and superior corporate profitability that fuelled a dazzling two-year bull run on Wall Street.

This so-called US exceptionalism, which has reigned supreme since the global financial crisis, attracted huge capital inflows – foreign investors entered this year with a record 18 per cent ownership of US stocks. Australian investors alone poured a record $5 billion into Wall Street-focused exchange-traded funds in the 12 months to December 31.

But that trend has violently reversed in the past few weeks with foreign investors selling an estimated $US60 billion ($93.2 billion) of US stocks since the start of March, according to Goldman Sachs.

Pendal investment analyst Elise McKay said a portion of that money is flowing into the local sharemarket, particularly large cap stocks.

That was evident last week as the S&P/ASX 20 rallied 2.5 per cent, outperforming the benchmark S&P/ASX 200 which climbed 1.9 per cent and the S&P/ASX Small Ordinaries which rose just 0.3 per cent.

“This is possibly an outcome from global asset managers reducing US equities exposure and up-weighting global exposures, of which Australia is a beneficiary,” McKay said.

The major banks, in particular, have surged following US President Donald Trump’s tariff announcement earlier this month, even as the broader market has seesawed.

“We feel the likely near-term deterioration in US economic performance warrants a more cautious stance on US equities.”

The S&P/ASX 200 Banks Index has rallied 12.2 per cent over the past three weeks, beating the benchmark index which is up 9.5 per cent over the same period. Commonwealth Bank shares hit a fresh record of $168.70 last week, which Bell Potter strategist Richard Coppleson partly attributed to a large institutional investor selling out of US stocks and moving into local shares.

Macquarie, in a note to its clients, said the market volatility sparked by US tariff plans – most of the imposts have been paused until July – have turned Australian banks “as a relative safe haven supporting performance”.

“Investor feedback and Macquarie proprietary flows data suggest offshore investors in particular have been moving into financials given their relatively limited impact from US tariffs,” the broker told its clients in a note. “Indeed, our data suggests that offshore investors increased their cumulative net buying of financials by 22 per cent since ‘liberation day’.”

Coming home

ECP Asset Management’s Manny Pohl believes Australia’s superannuation funds will increasingly rotate out of Wall Street and into the local sharemarket as they lose faith in the Trump administration.

“People will rethink the massive flow of money into the US because clearly Trump only thinks about the US and you can’t have people’s savings in a place that clearly doesn’t treat you the way you should be treated,” Pohl said.

“So I think a lot of that money will come back home into infrastructure, property and into our markets.”

Pohl, who previously founded Hyperion Asset Management before running ECP, picked up on that trend last year and subsequently looked beyond the magnificent technology stocks in ECP’s global fund.

Other money managers are following suit.

Wilsons Advisory told clients US equities may no longer be able to command a premium to their peers – Wall Street has traded at an average forward price-to-earnings ratio 40 per cent higher than the rest of the world.

“We feel the likely near-term deterioration in US economic performance warrants a more cautious stance on US equities and a broader diversification into non-US assets – including Australia,” said Wilsons’ head of investment strategy, David Cassidy.

Others such as local boutique manager Ten Cap are “reluctant to jump on the bandwagon” and dump US stocks. Ten Cap chief investment officer Jason Todd said the US still boasts the largest collection of high-quality growth companies in the world, superior profit margins and a flexible economy.

“At around 50 per cent of global market capitalisation, a diversified portfolio cannot afford to not be [in the US],” Todd said.

item.title: ASX hits two-month high, $A rallies; MinRes soars
item.description:
New CEO at wine group Australian Vintage

Wine company Australian Vintage has appointed Tom Dusseldorp as its new chief executive, promoting him from the role of chief commercial officer.

He replaces Craig Garvin, who had only rejoined the company as chief executive in October 2024.

Australian Vintage owns brands including McGuigan, Tempus Two and Nepenthe. It rehired Garvin in October after the previous board sacked him in May last year for a “lack of judgement”.

ASX, $A hit fresh highs; MinRes leaps 13pc

The Australian sharemarket closed at a two-month high on Tuesday, shrugging off a volatile session on Wall Street as hopes that US President Donald Trump will ease tariffs coincided with expectations of cooling inflation in Australia.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 0.9 per cent, or 73.5 points, to 8070.6 – its highest level in eight weeks and its fourth consecutive day of gains. Ten of 11 sectors were in the green, led by energy stocks.

Mixed messages on trade policy and investor caution drove a volatile session on Wall Street. The S&P 500 closed marginally higher, while technology stocks whipsawed ahead of earnings from Amazon, Microsoft and Meta this week.

The White House announced after Wall Street closed that tariffs on automotive manufacturers would be reduced, driving gains in the Australian sharemarket and across Asia. Gold dropped to nearly $US3300 an ounce, as demand for safe-haven assets waned.

Still, futures for the S&P 500 gained 0.1 per cent by the closing bell in Sydney, paring much of its rise earlier in the session.

A sustained bounce?

Ben Clark, a portfolio manager at TMS Private Wealth, warned that the Australian sharemarket’s advance was more likely a temporary “bounce” rather than a sustained rally, pointing to risks that could prompt a reversal.

“We did a lot of buying when the market hit its April 7 low, but now I’m a little more cautious,” he said. “History tells you to keep some powder dry and if there’s another leg lower from new tariff announcements, then we’d be buying again.”

“It wouldn’t take a lot for this bounce to fizzle out. Retesting lows is just what markets do,” he added.

Technology stocks advanced, with NextDC up 2.2 per cent to $11.65 and WiseTech 1.2 per cent to $87.60. The energy sector was buoyed by uranium plays after Boss Energy said its South Australian uranium project had generated its first quarter of free cash flow. The stock jumped 14.3 per cent to $3.20, while Deep Yellow rose 11.7 per cent to $1.15.

The Australian dollar climbed to a fresh 2025 peak of US64.49¢ as further confusion about Trump’s trade policies weighed on the greenback.

Hopes for a positive inflation reading in Australia on Wednesday also buoyed sentiment. The core consumer price index is expected to increase 0.7 per cent in the first quarter, taking the annual rate to within the Reserve Bank’s target range of 2 per cent to 3 per cent.

Stocks in focus

Mineral Resources rallied 13.2 per cent to $20.57 after the miner assured investors that it is not considering raising equity.

Northern Star Resources dropped 4.7 per cent to $19.88 after downgrading its full-year gold output guidance.

Whitehaven Coal rose 4.7 per cent to $5.08 as investors shrugged off a fall in its quarterly production and sales owing to seasonal weather impacts on its Queensland mine and slower-than-planned progress at its Narrabri operations.

Fortescue Metals advanced 5.8 per cent to $16.37 after Citi upgraded the iron ore miner to “neutral”, pointing to its “big underperformance” compared to peers.

Australian dollar scales fresh 2025 peak

The Australian dollar climbed to a fresh 2025 peak as further confusion in the White House’s trade policies weighed on the greenback. The Aussie hit US64.49¢, the highest since December 9. It has gained nearly 4 per cent this year.

UBS cuts ASX price target amid ‘softening fundamentals’

UBS has slashed its year-end target for the S&P/ASX 200 to 8150, from 8850 previously, implying the benchmark index will barely move from current levels.

Strategist Richard Schellbach said the ASX’s recent rebound has run ahead of “softening underlying fundamentals” and warned of a looming wave of earnings downgrades, which reflect the deteriorating global economic outlook.

“We expect the upcoming period of trading updates and quarterlies from Aussie companies to be unfavourable in both tone and guidance revisions, and thus expect to see earnings downgrades from consensus analysts,” Schellbach wrote in a note to clients.

UBS has reduced its risk exposure by upgrading healthcare stocks to a “neutral” rating and downgrading industrials to the same rating.

“We shift our sector strategy such that the overall risk of our portfolio is dialled back, alongside staying overweight on sectors where the earnings trajectory is somewhat agnostic to the macro environment such as insurance and technology, media, and telecom,” Schellbach said.

$A shorts hit 2025 low

Net short positions in the Australian dollar hit their lowest level this year as US President Donald Trump’s attacks on the Federal Reserve sparked an exodus from US assets.

Asset managers trimmed Australian dollar net shorts to just -5000 contracts in the week to April 22, from 12,000 the week prior. That was the fourth straight week net short positions fell and marked their least bearish position since October. Hedge fund shorts fell marginally to -22,600 contracts.

The dollar hit a year-to-date high of US64.39¢ on April 22, though its gain was one of the weakest amidst the major currencies that week.

Citi upgrades Fortescue

Citi has upgraded Fortescue Metals, pointing to the iron ore miner’s “big underperformance” compared to its peers.

Analyst Paul McTaggart upgraded the stock from “buy” to “neutral” following the iron ore miner’s quarterly production update on Tuesday that showed costs and performance fell in line with expectations.

That was despite net debt rising marginally on the prior quarter to $2.1 billion, in part owing to the acquisition of Red Hawk Mining.

McTaggart pointed to Fortescue’s 17 per cent share price decline in the past three months, underperforming BHP and Rio Tinto’s decline of around 2 per cent.

ASX holds two-month high; Paladin surges

The Australian sharemarket held a two-month high on Tuesday, shrugging off a volatile session on Wall Street as more easing in US tariffs and expectations for a cooling in inflation buoyed sentiment. US futures lifted.

The S&P/ASX 200 Index rose 1 per cent, or 79.2 points, to 8076.3 points near 2.40pm, its highest level in eight weeks. The All Ordinaries lifted 1.1 per cent. All 11 sectors were in the green, led by energy.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told journalists overnight that America is focusing on talks with nations other than China. US equities sold off early as the rally that helped the S&P 500 index clinch its best week this year lost steam, before turning marginally positive in late trade. The Nasdaq slipped 0.1 per cent.

The White House said after market close that it had reduced the impact of automotive tariffs by alleviating some duties imposed on foreign parts. “The tariff issue is not going away, but I think there’s been a realisation that the pace at which they were being enacted was too high for how fast the industry could adjust,” JPMorgan global market strategist Kerry Craig said.

Expectations for a positive inflation reading on Wednesday also helped buoy sentiment in Australia, pushing the dollar towards a year-to-date high. Quarterly consumer price index data on Wednesday is expected to show inflation coming back within the Reserve Bank’s 2 to 3 per cent target for the first time in four years.

Technology and real estate stocks advanced, with Xero up 1.5 per cent and WiseTech rising 1.2 per cent. Property stock Goodman Group was up 1.9 per cent and Mirvac 0.9 per cent.

Mineral Resources posted the biggest gain, up 13.6 per cent as investors shrugged off a disappointing quarterly report that slashed its iron ore output guidance.

Stocks on the move

Energy stocks were buoyed by uranium stocks, after producer Boss Energy said its South Australian uranium project had generated its first quarter of free cashflow. Deep Yellow rose 10.3 per cent and Paladin Energy 9.7 per cent, extending the latter’s five-day advance to 42.8 per cent.

In corporate news, Northern Star Resources weighed after downgrading its full-year gold output guidance. The stock fell 5.5 per cent, notching the biggest loss on the bourse.

Endeavour Group lifted 1 per cent after appointing Jayne Hrdlicka, the former chief executive of Virgin Australia, as its new CEO.

Whitehaven Coal rose 4.9 per cent as investors shrugged off a fall in its quarterly production and sales owing to seasonal weather impacts on its Queensland mine and slower-than-planned progress at Narrabri in NSW.

Auckland International Airport retreated 2.6 per cent after announcing it would delay building a second runway for at least 10 years.

Uranium stocks surge

Uranium stocks held on to sizeable gains in the afternoon session, buoyed by Boss Energy after its South Australian uranium project generated its first quarter of free cash flow.

Boss Energy advanced 11.8 per cent near 2pm to lead the gains. Deep Yellow rallied 10.7 per cent and Paladin 10.1 per cent.

Reporting quarterly earnings on Tuesday, Boss said 295,819 pounds of uranium oxide had been drummed from the Honeymoon project in the three months to March, up 116 per cent on the December quarter. That was sold at an average realised price of $133 a pound, with cash received for 268,000 pounds. Managing director Duncan Craib said that both output and costs had met or exceeded guidance.

Boss, Deep Yellow and Paladin were the second, third, and fourth best-performing stocks on the ASX 200 respectively near 2pm.

Jayne ‘Hard Liquor’ has a big job ahead

Dan Murphy’s owner Endeavour Group’s board has elected for a course of shock therapy in a bid to end a four-year fall from grace.

Former Virgin Australia boss Jayne Hrdlicka – already deliciously dubbed Jayne “Hard Liquor” – will administer it. She’s strategic, energetic, combative and divisive, and whichever way this proposed turnaround goes, it will not be boring.

By hiring Hrdlicka, Endeavour’s board has an unstoppable force to meet its immovable object – pubs baron Bruce Mathieson and his son Bruce jnr, who own 15.1 per cent of the company.

ASX 200 touches two-month high

The sharemarket briefly notched a two-month high near 12.45pm as a rally in the big banks and BHP gathered steam.

The S&P/ASX 200 touched an intraday high of 8067.60 – its highest level since March 7. BHP pushed the bourse higher – the stock rose 1.2 per cent – as did Westpac, up 1 per cent. ANZ pared an early loss to rise 0.6 per cent.

Betr says ‘all concerns’ addressed in PointsBet bid

Betr has lobbed a revised takeover proposal for bookmaker rival PointsBet, telling investors it had addressed all issues previously raised about the bid.

The development comes after Betr bought nearly 20 per cent of PointsBet shares on Monday, throwing a major curveball in Japanese entertainment giant Mixi’s takeover of the company.

Betr said on Tuesday that it would secure funding worth over $260 million, comprised of a $120 million loan from National Australia Bank, proceeds from the potential sale of its Canadian business and a $130 million fully underwritten equity raise.

The betting app provider also said its synergy estimates had been verified by a big four accounting firm. It also committed to a three-week confirmatory due diligence process, primarily to satisfy the requirements of the National Australia Bank loan.

Betr chairman Matthew Tripp said that the offer “represented a clearly superior proposal for PointsBet shareholders to realise significant value”.

“As the largest shareholder in PointsBet, we now intend to vote our holding against the current Mixi proposal, reducing its likelihood of success.”
